title: Load Testing: Finding the Knee Before Users Do
objectives: Pick load, stress, soak or spike tests for the question you are asking
Explain why open-model load generation reveals overload that closed-model tools hide
Find the throughput knee and turn it into a per-instance capacity target

cards.title: Four questions, four test shapes
cards.body: A load test checks the expected peak with some margin. A stress test raises load until something breaks, to find the limit and how it fails. A soak test holds normal load for hours to expose leaks, growing queues and log disks filling up. A spike test jumps load suddenly to check autoscaling, cold caches and connection limits. Pick the shape from the question, not from habit.

cards.title: Open vs closed load models
cards.body: A closed model runs a fixed number of virtual users, and each waits for its response before sending the next request. When the server slows down, the users send less, so the test quietly reduces the load it is meant to apply. An open model sends requests at a fixed arrival rate whatever happens, like real users on the internet, so overload shows up as growing queues and latency.

cards.title: Finding the knee
cards.body: Step the arrival rate and watch where throughput stops following it.
steps: Ramp the arrival rate in steps against one instance or a small fleet
Hold each step long enough for latency and queues to settle
Record throughput, error rate and p50 and p99 latency at each step
Throughput follows the offered load, then flattens at the knee
Past the knee, p99 shoots up and errors start as queues grow
Set the planning target well below the knee

cards.title: Worked example: a knee at 1,100 requests per second
cards.body: Illustrative results for one instance: p99 is 120 ms up to 800 requests per second, 250 ms at 1,000, and 2 s at 1,100, where throughput stops rising. Plan for 750 to 800 per instance, not 1,100, so normal noise and a slow dependency do not push it over. For a 6,000 requests per second peak at 750 each, that is 8 instances, plus spares for losing an instance or a zone.

cards.title: Trap: a closed-loop tool hides the stall
cards.body: If the server freezes for 5 seconds, a closed-loop tool records one slow response per virtual user and then carries on. The thousands of requests real users would have sent during the freeze are never sent, so they are missing from the percentiles. This is called coordinated omission. Use open-model generators, or measure latency from when each request was scheduled to go out, not when it was actually sent.

questions.prompt: Memory climbs slowly and the service crashes after about nine hours of normal traffic. Which test would have caught it?

choices.label: A spike test
A stress test
A soak test
A smoke test

questions.explanation: Soak tests hold normal load for hours, which is what exposes slow leaks. Spike and stress tests are short and push load up; a smoke test only checks that the basics work.

questions.prompt: Why can a closed-loop load test understate overload?

choices.label: Its virtual users wait for each response, so a slow server gets fewer requests
It sends requests much faster than real users would
It skips TLS, so each request is cheaper than in production
It reports only the median and drops the slow tail

questions.explanation: Waiting users self-throttle as the server slows. Sending too fast would overstate load, and TLS and reporting depend on how the tool is configured, not on the closed model.

questions.prompt: Throughput stops rising at 1,100 requests per second, while p99 jumps from 250 ms to 2 s. What per-instance planning target makes sense?

choices.label: 1,100 requests per second, the highest rate measured
About 800 requests per second, well below the knee
1,500 requests per second, since autoscaling covers the rest
The average of every rate that was tested

questions.explanation: Plan below the knee so noise and slow dependencies leave headroom. At 1,100 the instance is already saturated, 1,500 is beyond what it can serve at all, and the average of the tested rates says nothing about the system.

questions.prompt: A service freezes for 5 seconds once, and a closed-loop tool records a single 5 s sample per virtual user. Why does that understate the damage?

choices.label: The tool rounds long samples down to its configured timeout
Requests real users would have sent during the freeze are missing
A few slow samples among many cannot move any percentile
Freezes are filtered out by the tool as network noise

questions.explanation: The tool stopped sending while it waited, so the freeze looks like a few slow requests rather than thousands. Rounding and filtering depend on settings, and enough slow samples do move the tail percentiles.

questions.prompt: Peak traffic is 6,000 requests per second. Each instance is planned at 750 requests per second, below its knee, and you keep 2 spare instances. How many instances in total?
assumptions: Load spreads evenly
Spares are on top of the peak need
questions.explanation: Sanity check: sizing at the knee of 1,100 would give 6 instances, which leaves no room for a slow dependency or a lost instance.

questions.prompt: Order a stepped load test that finds the knee.

items.label: Find where throughput flattens and p99 climbs
Pick the arrival-rate steps
Set the planning target below that point
Record throughput, errors and p99 per step
Hold each step until latency settles

questions.explanation: Plan, hold, measure, locate the knee, and leave headroom under it.

flashcards.back: Soak: normal load for hours, finds leaks. Spike: a sudden jump, tests scaling and limits.
Open sends at a fixed arrival rate; closed users wait for responses and self-throttle.
Missing samples during a stall because the tool waited; measure from the scheduled send time.

sources.title: Google SRE book: Testing for Reliability
Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Load Testing?

mechanism.title: How to run a load test you can trust
steps: Start from the question. “Can we handle the festival-sale peak?” needs a load test at the forecast peak plus margin. “Where do we break, and how?” needs a stress test. “Do we leak over a day?” needs a soak test. “Do autoscaling, cold caches and connection limits survive a sudden jump?” needs a spike test. Each has a different shape, duration and success criterion.

Generate load the way users do. Real users arrive independently of how fast your server is, so an open model, a fixed arrival rate, reproduces overload honestly. A closed model with a fixed number of virtual users is useful for modelling a known pool of clients, such as a batch of workers, but it reduces its own load as latency rises and can make a saturated system look healthy.

Measure at each step after it settles: throughput actually served, error rate, and latency percentiles, especially p99. Throughput tracks offered load until a resource saturates, such as CPU, a thread or connection pool, a database or a lock, and then flattens. That bend is the knee. Past it, queues grow, p99 climbs steeply and timeouts begin. Record which resource saturated, because that is the next thing to fix or scale.

Measure latency from when each request was meant to be sent. If the generator waits during a stall and sends late, the stall’s full effect is lost: coordinated omission. Check that the load generator itself is not the bottleneck by watching its CPU and network, and run it close enough to the system that its own latency does not dominate. Use production-like data sizes, caches that start cold as they would after a deploy, and realistic request mixes.

Turn the knee into planning numbers. A per-instance target well below the knee, often 60 to 75% of it, leaves room for noise, slow dependencies and uneven load balancing. Divide the forecast peak by the target, add spares for instance or zone loss, and rerun the test after significant changes, because the knee moves when code, dependencies or instance types change.

useWhen: Before launches, big sales or marketing events, and after major architecture changes.
To set autoscaling thresholds and per-instance capacity targets from evidence.
avoidWhen: Avoid testing against shared production dependencies without their owners’ agreement.
Avoid trusting results when the load generator was saturated or the data set was tiny.

rows: Do we meet the SLO at peak?
Where and how do we break?
Do we survive a sudden jump?
Low, then a sharp step up

numbers.title: From a knee to a fleet size
assumptions: Knee measured at 1,100 requests per second per instance
Planning target 70% of the knee
Forecast peak 7,000 requests per second; illustrative numbers
steps: Target per instance: 1,100 × 0.7 = 770 requests per second.
Instances for the peak: 7,000 ÷ 770 ≈ 9.1, round up to 10.
Survive a zone loss in a three-zone fleet: 10 ÷ 2 = 5 per zone, 15 instances in total.
numbers.result: Plan from the knee with headroom, then add the spare that a zone loss needs, the same arithmetic as the zone lesson.

india.title: Overload guidance from Google SRE
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Google SRE book’s chapter on handling overload explains that queries per second is a poor capacity measure when request cost varies, and recommends measuring capacity in terms of the resource that actually limits the service and degrading gracefully past it. Its chapter on testing for reliability covers load and stress testing as part of release confidence. Azure Load Testing documents running scripted tests at scale with server-side metrics.

pitfalls.trap: “Our test ran 500 users and latency looked fine.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check whether it was an open model; closed users slow down with the server and hide the overload.”

pitfalls.trap: “The instance maxed out at 1,100, so we plan for 1,100.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d plan around 70–75% of the knee and add spares for losing a zone.”

takeaways: Pick load, stress, soak or spike from the question you need answered.
Use an open arrival-rate model; closed users self-throttle.
Find the knee where throughput flattens and p99 climbs; plan well below it.
Measure latency from the scheduled send time to avoid coordinated omission.

interactive.title: Push one instance past its knee
interactive.prompt: One instance serves at most 1,100 requests per second, and clients give up after 2 s. Slide the offered load of an open-model test and watch the queue after 30 seconds.
interactive.takeaway: Below 1,100 nothing queues. At 1,200 the queue grows by 100 a second, waits pass the 2 s timeout after about 22 s, and the instance ends up working on answers nobody reads. A closed-model test would hide this, because its users would have slowed down.

title: Service Mesh: Sidecars, mTLS and When It Pays Off
objectives: Describe the data plane and control plane of a service mesh
Explain how mesh mTLS gives each call a verifiable workload identity
Spot retry and timeout conflicts between the app and the mesh, and judge when a mesh is worth its cost

cards.title: Networking moved out of the app
cards.body: A service mesh puts a proxy in the path of every call between services: a sidecar container next to each workload, or a shared proxy per node. The proxies form the data plane and handle encryption, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and metrics the same way for every language. A control plane sends them configuration and certificates. Proxies keep using their last configuration if the control plane is briefly unavailable.

cards.title: One call through the mesh
cards.body: The app sends a plain request; both proxies do the rest.
steps: The app calls another service by name over a plain local connection
Its proxy picks a healthy endpoint and applies the timeout and retry policy
The proxy opens mutual TLS to the destination proxy with a short-lived workload certificate
The destination proxy checks the caller’s identity against the authorisation policy
It forwards the request to the destination app on the local host
Both proxies emit metrics and trace spans for the call

cards.title: Worked example: retries in two layers multiply
cards.body: The app retries a failed call twice, and the mesh is also set to retry twice. One user request can now reach the downstream service (1 + 2) × (1 + 2) = 9 times. During an outage that becomes nine times the load on a struggling dependency. Decide which layer owns retries, make the inner layer’s total time fit inside the outer deadline, and cap retries with a budget.

cards.title: What mTLS adds over a firewall rule
cards.body: A network rule says which addresses may connect. Mesh mTLS says which workload is calling: each proxy holds a certificate naming its service identity, issued and rotated by the control plane, often every few hours. Policies can then allow “orders may call payments” whatever pod addresses either side has, and every connection inside the cluster is encrypted.

cards.title: Trap: a mesh for three services
cards.body: Every sidecar costs CPU and memory, adds a hop of latency, and the mesh brings its own upgrades and failure modes. For a handful of services in one language, a shared client library and platform-level TLS may do the job. A mesh pays off with many services, several languages, and a requirement for uniform mTLS, traffic control and telemetry.

questions.prompt: In a sidecar mesh, what actually carries a request from one service to another?

choices.label: The control plane, which forwards each request
The cluster DNS server, which relays the call
The proxies running next to each workload
The ingress gateway at the edge of the cluster

questions.explanation: The sidecar proxies are the data plane. The control plane only configures them, DNS only resolves names, and the ingress gateway handles traffic entering the cluster.

questions.prompt: The mesh control plane is down for ten minutes. What happens to calls between running services?

choices.label: They stop, because each call needs control-plane approval
They keep flowing with the last configuration the proxies received
They fall back to plain text with no encryption
They are rerouted through the ingress gateway

questions.explanation: Proxies are statically stable on their last config; new config, new workloads and certificate rotation wait until the control plane returns. Calls are not approved one by one, not downgraded, and not sent through the gateway.

questions.prompt: What does mesh mTLS give that a network firewall rule alone does not?

choices.label: Faster connections, because encryption is moved to hardware
Each call carries a verified workload identity that policy can check
Protection against bugs in the application’s own business logic
Validation of every request body against a published schema

questions.explanation: mTLS proves which workload is calling, so policy can use identities instead of addresses. It adds some cost rather than speed, and it does not inspect business logic or request bodies.

questions.prompt: The app gives each call a 2,000 ms deadline. The mesh may make up to 3 tries in total for that call. What is the longest per-try timeout that keeps all three tries inside the app deadline?
assumptions: Retries start immediately, with no backoff
Every try runs to its full timeout
questions.explanation: Design implication: a 1,000 ms per-try timeout would need 3,000 ms, so the app abandons the call during the third try, and a 2,000 ms per-try timeout makes the mesh retries pointless.

questions.prompt: Which situation most justifies adopting a service mesh?

choices.label: Three services in one language that already share a client library
Hundreds of services in several languages that all need mTLS
A single monolith behind one external load balancer
A nightly batch job that reads files and writes a report

questions.explanation: Uniform mTLS and telemetry across many services and languages is where a mesh saves the most work. A few same-language services can share a library, and a monolith or a batch job has few service-to-service calls to manage.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when one service calls another through the mesh.

items.label: Proxies set up mutual TLS with workload certificates
The request reaches the destination app
The app sends a plain request to the service name
The destination proxy authorises the caller
The local proxy picks an endpoint and applies policy

questions.explanation: Plain locally, policy at the source proxy, mTLS between proxies, authorisation at the destination, then the app.

flashcards.back: Proxies carry traffic; the control plane configures them and issues certificates.
They multiply: (1 + app retries) × (1 + mesh retries). Let one layer own retries.

flashcards.front: When is a mesh worth it?
flashcards.back: Many services, several languages, and a need for uniform mTLS, traffic control and telemetry.

sources.title: Google Cloud: Cloud Service Mesh overview

mechanism.title: How a service mesh handles each call
steps: In the classic design, each pod gets a sidecar proxy, and traffic in and out of the app is redirected through it, usually by network rules set up when the pod starts. Newer designs move some work to a shared proxy per node and add per-service proxies only where layer-7 features are needed, which cuts the per-pod cost. Either way the app speaks plain HTTP or gRPC to a local proxy and needs no mesh library.

The control plane watches the cluster for services and endpoints, turns routing, retry and security policies into proxy configuration, and pushes it out. It also acts as a certificate authority: each workload gets a short-lived certificate that encodes its service identity, rotated on a schedule. Proxies cache their configuration, so a control-plane outage stops changes and the setup of new workloads, but existing traffic keeps flowing.

Between proxies, connections use mutual TLS. Both sides present certificates, so the destination proxy knows which workload is calling and can enforce policies such as “only the orders service may call payments, and only with POST”. That moves service-to-service authorisation from IP-based firewall rules, which break as pods move, to identities that follow the workload.

Traffic policy is where meshes help and hurt. Timeouts, retries with budgets, outlier detection that ejects failing endpoints, and weighted traffic splits for canaries are applied the same way for every service. But they stack with whatever the application already does: two layers of retries multiply attempts, and mesh retries that need longer than the app’s overall deadline are retries nobody waits for. Decide which layer owns each behaviour.

The costs are real. Every proxy reserves CPU and memory, which across hundreds of pods adds up to whole machines. Each call takes extra hops through two proxies, adding latency that should be measured rather than assumed. The mesh itself must be upgraded, monitored and debugged, and a bad policy push can break many services at once. Adopt it when uniform security, traffic control and telemetry are worth that operating load.

useWhen: Many services in several languages that need mTLS, consistent telemetry and traffic control.
Zero-trust requirements where calls must be authorised by workload identity.
avoidWhen: Avoid for a few services or a monolith, where a shared library or platform TLS is simpler.
Avoid adopting it only for metrics that existing instrumentation already provides.

rows: Retries and metrics in one language
Less per-pod cost; one proxy shared per node

numbers.title: What the sidecars cost
assumptions: 400 pods, each with a sidecar requesting 0.1 vCPU and 64 MiB
Illustrative request sizes; measure your own proxies
steps: CPU: 400 × 0.1 = 40 vCPU reserved for proxies.
Memory: 400 × 64 MiB = 25,600 MiB, which is 25 GiB.
With 8-vCPU nodes, 40 ÷ 8 = 5 whole nodes’ worth of CPU goes to the mesh.
numbers.result: At scale the mesh costs several machines; that is fine if it replaces work every team would otherwise do, and wasteful if it does not.

india.title: Provider guidance on meshes
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Microsoft’s AKS documentation describes a service mesh as adding capabilities such as traffic management, mTLS-based security and observability, and suggests evaluating your requirements before adopting one. Google Cloud Service Mesh documentation describes a managed control plane that configures proxies for traffic management, mutual TLS and telemetry. Both present the mesh as an option with an operating cost, not a default.

pitfalls.trap: “A mesh makes services reliable because it retries everything.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d let one layer own retries with a budget, because app and mesh retries multiply load during an outage.”

pitfalls.trap: “We need a mesh for our three services.”
pitfalls.say: “For three services in one language I’d start with a shared client and platform TLS, and revisit a mesh as we grow.”

takeaways: Proxies are the data plane; the control plane configures them and issues certificates.
Mesh mTLS gives each call a verified workload identity for policy.
App and mesh retries multiply; one layer should own them.
A mesh pays off with many services and languages, not with a few.

interactive.title: Two timeouts, one hung dependency
interactive.prompt: The app gives each call to the inventory service a 2 s deadline. The mesh retries a failed or slow call up to 3 times in total, with 1 s per try. Inventory hangs completely.

choices.label: The app gives up at 2 s while the mesh starts its third try, which adds load nobody waits for
choices.feedback: Right: the mesh needs up to 3 s, the app waits only 2 s, so the outer deadline ends first.

choices.label: The user waits about 3 s while the mesh finishes all three tries
choices.feedback: The app’s own 2 s deadline ends the request before the mesh is done.

choices.label: The user gets an error after 1 s, when the first mesh try times out
choices.feedback: The mesh retries after the first try instead of returning the error.

interactive.reveal: Make the inner layer’s total time fit inside the outer deadline, for example 2 tries of 0.8 s, or let only one layer retry.

seeAlso.why: How services find each other before a mesh routes the call
Retry and timeout rules the mesh applies for you
Authentication and authorisation, the ideas behind workload identity

title: Kubernetes Scheduling: Placement, Taints and Topology Spread
objectives: Explain how the scheduler filters and scores nodes using requests, not live usage
Steer pods onto or away from nodes with selectors, affinity, taints and tolerations
Spread replicas across zones with topology spread constraints, and predict preemption

cards.title: Filter, then score
cards.body: For each pending pod the scheduler first filters out nodes that cannot run it: not enough unreserved CPU or memory for its requests, a taint it does not tolerate, a node selector or affinity rule it fails, a volume in another zone. It then scores the nodes that remain, for example preferring spread or less-loaded nodes, and binds the pod to the best one. Requests are what count, not current usage: a node at 20% CPU can still be full if its pods have reserved all of it.

cards.title: Attract and repel: affinity, taints and tolerations
cards.body: A node selector or node affinity pulls a pod towards nodes with certain labels, such as a GPU type or a zone. A taint on a node pushes pods away: only pods with a matching toleration may land there. They solve different halves of the problem. To reserve GPU nodes for GPU jobs, taint the GPU nodes so other pods stay off, and give GPU jobs both the toleration and an affinity so they actually go there. A toleration alone only permits a node; it does not choose it.

cards.title: How one pod is placed
cards.body: The scheduler only ever reasons about declared requests and rules.
steps: A pod is created with requests, tolerations and spread rules
Filter: drop nodes without enough unreserved requests
Filter: drop tainted nodes the pod does not tolerate, and nodes failing affinity
Filter: drop nodes that would break a hard topology spread rule
Score the rest, for example preferring balance across zones
Bind the pod to the best node; the kubelet starts it

cards.title: Worked example: nine replicas, three zones
cards.body: A Deployment of 9 replicas has a topology spread constraint on the zone label with a maximum skew of 1, so no zone may have more than one pod above another: 3, 3, 3. If zone C fails, its 3 pods are recreated; with the rule set to schedule anyway, they land in A and B, giving 5 and 4. Each node has 7.5 vCPU allocatable and each pod requests 1 vCPU, so a node fits 7 pods, and the remaining zones need enough spare requests for the extra pods, or the replacements stay Pending.

cards.title: Trap: Pending pods on idle-looking nodes
cards.body: Dashboards show nodes at 20% CPU while new pods stay Pending with “insufficient cpu”. The pods already on those nodes request far more than they use, so the scheduler sees the nodes as full. Fix requests from measured usage, and let a cluster autoscaler add nodes when pods are Pending. Adding a CPU limit does not help, because the scheduler places pods by requests, not limits.

cards.title: When the cluster is full: priority and preemption
cards.body: Pods can carry a priority class. When a high-priority pod cannot fit anywhere, the scheduler may preempt: it evicts lower-priority pods from a node to make room, trying to respect their disruption budgets, though it cannot promise to. This keeps critical workloads running during a squeeze, but a careless high default priority lets ordinary deploys evict each other.

questions.prompt: New pods stay Pending with “0/6 nodes available: insufficient cpu”, yet every node shows about 20% CPU in use. What is the most likely cause?

choices.label: The metrics pipeline is down, so the scheduler cannot see the real usage
Existing pods request much more CPU than they use
The CPU limits on the new pods are set lower than their requests
The nodes need a restart before they accept new pods

questions.explanation: The scheduler adds up requests, not usage, so over-sized requests make idle nodes look full. It never reads live metrics for placement, a limit below a request is rejected when the pod is created rather than leaving it Pending, and restarting nodes frees no requests.

questions.prompt: Expensive GPU nodes keep filling up with ordinary web pods. What keeps them for GPU jobs?

choices.label: Add a node selector for the GPU label to the GPU jobs only
Taint the GPU nodes, and give GPU jobs a toleration and affinity
Give the GPU jobs a higher priority class than the web pods
Move the GPU jobs into a namespace of their own

questions.explanation: Only a taint repels other pods; the toleration lets GPU jobs in and affinity sends them there. A selector on GPU jobs does not stop web pods landing on GPU nodes, priority only matters when the cluster is full, and namespaces do not control which nodes pods run on.

questions.prompt: All 6 replicas of a service ended up in one zone, and a zone outage took it down. What fix targets the cause?

choices.label: Pod anti-affinity on the hostname label so no two replicas share a node
A disruption budget that keeps at least 4 replicas running
A topology spread constraint on the zone label with a skew of 1
Raising the replica count to 12 so more of them survive

questions.explanation: Spreading on the zone label keeps replicas balanced across zones. Hostname anti-affinity spreads across nodes that may all sit in one zone, a disruption budget only limits voluntary evictions, and 12 replicas can still all land in the same zone.

questions.prompt: The cluster is full and a pod with a high priority class is Pending. What does the scheduler try?

choices.label: Evicting lower-priority pods on a node so that the new pod fits
Throttling the CPU of other pods until the new pod’s request fits
Holding the pod until another pod on some node exits by itself
Placing the pod anyway and letting the node overcommit its memory

questions.explanation: That is preemption: lower-priority pods are evicted, with their disruption budgets respected where possible. Throttling and overcommit do not create schedulable requests, and waiting is what happens to pods without enough priority to preempt.

questions.prompt: A node has 7.5 vCPU and 30 GiB of allocatable capacity. Each pod requests 1 vCPU and 2 GiB of memory. How many of these pods fit on the node?
assumptions: Nothing else runs on the node
Only requests count for placement
questions.workedAnswer: CPU allows 7 pods, memory allows 15, so 7 pods
questions.explanation: Sanity check: CPU is the binding resource here, so half the node’s memory sits unrequested; a pod shape that requests 0.5 vCPU and 4 GiB would pack this node better.

questions.prompt: A payments API runs 9 replicas in a three-zone cluster and must survive a zone loss.
constraints: Each zone has room for only 2 extra pods
Losing a zone must not drop below 6 replicas
Deploys must not stall on spread rules

approaches.label: Zone spread with skew 1, scheduling anyway if the rule cannot be met, plus spare capacity per zone
Zone spread with skew 1 that refuses to schedule if the rule cannot be met
No spread rule; rely on the scheduler’s default scoring

rationaleOptions.label: Replicas start balanced, so a zone loss removes only about a third
A hard rule is always safer because it never allows imbalance
Replacements still schedule into the surviving zones after a loss
Default scoring spreads replicas across zones reliably on its own

rationaleConflicts.r3: After a zone loss a hard rule can leave replacements Pending, because two zones cannot stay within a skew of 1 of a zone with no capacity.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Default scoring only prefers spread; under pressure it can still pack replicas into one zone.

questions.explanation: Balance replicas with a zone spread rule, but let it bend after a failure and keep headroom so the surviving zones can absorb the replacements.

flashcards.back: Requests, not live usage; a busy-looking or idle-looking node is irrelevant.
A taint repels pods without a toleration; affinity attracts pods to labelled nodes. Use both to dedicate nodes.
No topology domain, such as a zone, may hold more than one matching pod above another.

mechanism.title: How the scheduler decides where a pod runs
steps: The scheduler watches for pods with no node assigned. For each one it runs a filtering phase that removes every node where the pod cannot run, then a scoring phase that ranks the rest, and finally binds the pod to the highest-scoring node. If no node passes filtering, the pod stays Pending and an event explains which filter failed on how many nodes, which is the first thing to read when debugging.

Resource filtering compares the pod’s requests with each node’s allocatable capacity minus the requests of pods already bound there. Allocatable is less than the machine size because the operating system, the kubelet and system daemons reserve some. Live usage is not considered, so over-requesting wastes capacity and under-requesting packs nodes until pods contend or are evicted. Requests should come from measured usage at a high percentile.

Placement rules come in two directions. Node selectors and node affinity attract a pod to nodes with labels, as hard requirements or soft preferences. Taints repel: a tainted node accepts only pods that tolerate the taint, which is how dedicated node pools, GPU nodes and control-plane nodes are kept clear. Pod affinity and anti-affinity place pods relative to other pods, for example keeping a cache next to its clients or two replicas off the same node.

Topology spread constraints balance matching pods across a topology key such as the zone or hostname label. maxSkew bounds the difference between the fullest and emptiest domain. The whenUnsatisfiable setting chooses between refusing to schedule, which keeps balance strict but can leave pods Pending after a failure, and scheduling anyway while preferring balance. Spread across zones is what turns a multi-zone cluster into multi-zone resilience for a given service.

When nothing fits, two mechanisms act. A cluster autoscaler sees Pending pods and adds nodes from a node group that would fit them. Priority and preemption let a higher-priority pod evict lower-priority ones from a node so it can run, which keeps critical system and production pods alive during a squeeze. Preemption tries to respect disruption budgets but cannot guarantee it, so priority classes should be few and deliberate.

useWhen: Clusters shared by several teams or workload types, where placement must be predictable.
Services that must survive a zone or node loss, and expensive node types that must stay dedicated.
avoidWhen: Avoid hard affinity and spread rules that can leave pods Pending when capacity is tight.
Avoid many priority classes or a high default priority; deploys then preempt each other.

A toleration alone does not attract
Balances pods across zones or nodes

9 replicas over 3 zones, 1 node per zone, illustrative

india.title: Scheduling rules in the Kubernetes docs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Kubernetes documentation describes scheduling as filtering then scoring, and documents taints and tolerations, node affinity, inter-pod affinity, topology spread constraints and priority with preemption as the main placement controls. It notes that preemption tries to respect disruption budgets but cannot guarantee it, and that topology spread can either refuse to schedule or schedule anyway when the skew cannot be met.

pitfalls.trap: “The node is at 20% CPU, so the pod should fit.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d compare requests with allocatable; the scheduler only counts what pods reserve.”

pitfalls.trap: “We added a toleration, so GPU jobs will run on GPU nodes.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d add node affinity too, because a toleration only allows a node, it does not pick it.”

takeaways: The scheduler filters and scores nodes on requests, not live usage.
Taints keep pods off; affinity draws pods on; dedicate nodes with both.
Spread replicas across zones and keep spare requests per zone for a loss.
Priority lets critical pods preempt; keep classes few and deliberate.

interactive.title: Dedicated nodes that are not dedicated
interactive.prompt: You add a toleration for the gpu=true taint to your training jobs, but you do not taint any nodes and add no affinity. A week later the training jobs are running on ordinary nodes and web pods are on the GPU nodes.

choices.label: Expected: without a taint nothing is repelled, and without affinity nothing is attracted
choices.feedback: Right: a toleration only matters on a tainted node, and nothing told the jobs where to go.

choices.label: A bug: a toleration should pull the jobs onto the GPU nodes
choices.feedback: Tolerations permit; they do not attract. That is the job of node affinity or a selector.

choices.label: The scheduler ignores tolerations unless the pods also have a high priority
choices.feedback: Priority is unrelated to tolerations; it only matters when the cluster is full.

interactive.reveal: Taint the GPU nodes so other pods stay off, and give the training jobs both the toleration and a node affinity for the GPU label.

title: Kubernetes Networking: Services, Gateways and Network Policies
objectives: Explain how a Service gives pods a stable name and virtual IP, and why it balances connections rather than requests
Choose between LoadBalancer Services and a shared Ingress or Gateway for outside traffic
Write network policies that default-deny without breaking DNS

cards.title: Services: a stable name in front of moving pods
cards.body: Pods come and go with new addresses, so clients never call pods directly. A Service selects pods by label and gets a stable virtual IP and a DNS name such as orders.shop.svc.cluster.local. The cluster keeps a list of the ready pods behind it, its endpoints, and the node networking layer forwards each new connection to the virtual IP to one of them. Only ready pods are listed, which is how readiness probes take a pod out of rotation.

cards.title: Misconception: a Service balances every request
cards.body: The virtual IP is balanced per connection, not per request. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive and especially HTTP/2 or gRPC reuse one connection for thousands of requests, so a few clients holding long-lived connections can pin all their traffic to a few pods while the rest sit idle. Fixes are client-side balancing over the endpoint list, a proxy or mesh that balances per request, or limiting connection lifetime so connections are rebalanced.

cards.title: From the internet to a pod
cards.body: One shared entry point routes by host and path, then Services pick pods.
steps: The client resolves shop.example.com to the cloud load balancer
The load balancer forwards to the gateway or ingress controller pods
The gateway terminates TLS and matches the host and path rules
The matching route names a backend Service
The Service’s endpoints list only ready pods
The connection reaches one ready pod

cards.title: Getting traffic in: LoadBalancer, Ingress and Gateway
cards.body: A Service of type LoadBalancer asks the cloud for a load balancer per Service, which is simple but costs one load balancer and one address for each. Ingress and its successor, the Gateway API, put one shared layer 7 entry point in front of many Services, routing by hostname and path and terminating TLS in one place. The Gateway API splits the roles: the platform team owns the Gateway and its listeners, and app teams attach their own HTTP routes to it.

cards.title: Network policies: default allow until you say otherwise
cards.body: By default every pod can reach every other pod. A network policy selects pods and lists the traffic allowed in or out; once any policy selects a pod for a direction, everything not allowed in that direction is dropped. Policies only work if the cluster’s network plugin enforces them. A common baseline is a default-deny policy per namespace, then small policies that allow, say, frontend to api on port 8080.

cards.title: Trap: default-deny egress breaks DNS
cards.body: A team adds a default-deny egress policy and every service starts failing with name-resolution errors, not connection errors. The pods can no longer reach the cluster DNS service, so no name resolves at all. Any egress policy needs an explicit allow to the DNS pods on port 53 over both UDP and TCP, alongside the destinations each workload really needs.

questions.prompt: What does a ClusterIP Service give the clients inside the cluster?

choices.label: An address that is reachable from the public internet
A stable virtual IP and DNS name for ready pods
A proxy that retries a failed request on another pod
A single pod chosen to handle all of the service’s traffic

questions.explanation: A ClusterIP is internal and stable, and forwards connections to ready pods behind it. It is not public, and it does not retry requests or pin traffic to one pod; retries per request need a client library, a proxy or a mesh.

questions.prompt: A policy allows ingress to the api pods only from pods labelled app=frontend. What happens to a request from a batch pod to api?

choices.label: It is allowed, because policies only log traffic they do not list
It is allowed, because batch runs in the same namespace as api
It is dropped, along with traffic from the frontend pods
It is dropped, because api now only accepts traffic from frontend

questions.explanation: Once a policy selects the api pods for ingress, only listed sources get in, so batch is dropped and frontend is still allowed. Policies enforce rather than log, and being in the same namespace grants nothing once a policy applies.

questions.prompt: After a default-deny egress policy is applied, every service fails with “could not resolve host”. What is the fix?

choices.label: Allow egress to the cluster DNS pods on port 53 over UDP and TCP
Switch the services to call each other by pod IP addresses
Add an ingress policy that allows traffic into the DNS pods
Restart the DNS pods so they pick up the new policy

questions.explanation: The pods’ own egress to DNS is blocked, so an egress allow to the DNS pods on port 53 restores resolution. Pod IPs change, so hard-coding them breaks on the next reschedule; DNS pods accept traffic already, and restarting them does not change the client-side block.

questions.prompt: Twenty HTTP services each need a public hostname with TLS. Which setup keeps cost and operations down?

choices.label: One Service of type LoadBalancer for each of the twenty services
A NodePort per service, with each node’s IP in public DNS records
One shared Gateway or Ingress routing by hostname to each Service
A ClusterIP per service with traffic sent straight to pod addresses

questions.explanation: One shared layer 7 entry point handles TLS and routes by hostname, so you run one load balancer instead of twenty. Twenty LoadBalancer Services cost twenty load balancers, public node IPs break when nodes change, and ClusterIPs and pod addresses are not reachable from outside.

questions.prompt: Four client pods each hold one long-lived HTTP/2 connection to a ClusterIP Service with 10 ready server pods. At most how many server pods receive traffic?
assumptions: Each client opens one connection and reuses it for every request
Connections are never closed during the period
questions.explanation: Design implication: 6 of the 10 pods sit idle while 4 run hot, so balance per request with a client library or proxy, or cap connection lifetime so connections spread again.

questions.prompt: Order the hops a browser request takes to reach a pod behind a Gateway.

items.label: The gateway terminates TLS and matches a route
The Service forwards the connection to a ready pod
DNS resolves the hostname to the cloud load balancer
The route sends it to a backend Service
The load balancer forwards to the gateway pods

questions.explanation: Name, edge load balancer, layer 7 routing, Service, pod: each hop narrows where the request goes.

flashcards.back: Connections, not requests; long-lived HTTP/2 connections can pin traffic to a few pods.
Both give one shared layer 7 entry; the Gateway API is the successor, with roles split between platform and app teams.
Allow DNS: egress to the cluster DNS pods on port 53, UDP and TCP.

sources.title: Kubernetes: DNS for Services and Pods

mechanism.title: How traffic finds pods inside and into a cluster
steps: Every pod gets its own IP address on a flat cluster network, and any pod can reach any other without NAT. The network plugin implements this, using routes, overlays or the cloud’s own network, depending on the plugin. Pod addresses change whenever pods are rescheduled, so nothing should depend on them.

A Service selects pods by label. The control plane keeps EndpointSlices listing the ready pods, and each node programs forwarding rules, through kube-proxy or an eBPF-based plugin, so that a connection to the Service’s virtual IP is sent to one endpoint. The choice is made once per connection. Cluster DNS gives each Service a name of the form service.namespace.svc.cluster.local, and pods usually use the short name within their namespace.

Outside traffic needs an entry point. A Service of type LoadBalancer provisions a cloud load balancer per Service and suits a few TCP services. For many HTTP services, an Ingress or a Gateway gives one shared layer 7 entry: a controller runs proxy pods behind one load balancer, terminates TLS and routes by hostname and path to Services. The Ingress API is stable but no longer gaining features; the Gateway API is its successor, with GatewayClass, Gateway and route resources owned by different roles.

Network policies are allow lists. A pod no policy selects accepts and sends anything. When a policy selects it for ingress or egress, only traffic that some policy allows in that direction passes, and policies add up rather than override each other. Rules match pods by label, namespaces by label, or IP blocks, plus ports. Enforcement is done by the network plugin, so a cluster whose plugin lacks policy support accepts policies and silently ignores them.

A practical rollout is default-deny per namespace for ingress, then explicit allows between tiers, then egress control for sensitive workloads. Egress policies must allow DNS first, then the specific destinations each workload needs, such as the database and a payment API’s address range. Test policies in staging with real traffic, because a missing rule shows up as timeouts or resolution failures, not a clear error.

useWhen: Clusters with many HTTP services that need hostnames, TLS and routing in one place.
Multi-team or regulated clusters where lateral movement between pods must be limited.
avoidWhen: Avoid a LoadBalancer Service per HTTP service when one shared gateway would do.
Avoid relying on network policies before confirming the network plugin enforces them.

rows: A few TCP or UDP services
A controller to run and upgrade
Rules to maintain, needs plugin support

numbers.title: Connection pinning on a Service
assumptions: 10 server pods behind a ClusterIP Service
4 client pods, each with one long-lived HTTP/2 connection
Each client sends 500 requests per second, illustrative
steps: Total load: 4 × 500 = 2,000 requests per second.
With per-connection balancing, at most 4 pods serve it: 2,000 ÷ 4 = 500 requests per second each.
With per-request balancing over 10 pods: 2,000 ÷ 10 = 200 requests per second each.
numbers.result: The same traffic is 2.5 times hotter per pod when long-lived connections pin it, which is why gRPC services balance per request in the client or a proxy.

india.title: Services, gateways and policies in the docs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Kubernetes documentation describes Services as a stable virtual IP and DNS name backed by EndpointSlices of ready pods, and notes that the Ingress API is frozen while the Gateway API is the recommended successor for new features. Its network policy page states that pods are non-isolated by default, that policies are additive, and that a network plugin which supports NetworkPolicy is required for them to have any effect.

pitfalls.trap: “The Service load-balances, so every pod gets equal traffic.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check for long-lived connections; a Service balances per connection, not per request.”

pitfalls.trap: “We applied default-deny; the cluster is locked down.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d confirm the network plugin enforces policies and that DNS egress is still allowed.”

takeaways: A Service gives ready pods a stable name and virtual IP, balanced per connection.
Use one shared Gateway or Ingress for many HTTP services, not a load balancer each.
Network policies are additive allow lists; selected pods drop everything else.
Allow DNS egress first, and confirm the plugin enforces policies.

interactive.title: The gRPC service with idle pods
interactive.prompt: A gRPC service is scaled from 4 to 12 pods during a traffic spike. Its 3 client pods each hold one long-lived connection through a ClusterIP Service. Latency does not improve.

choices.label: The 3 existing connections still pin all traffic to at most 3 pods
choices.feedback: Right: new pods only get connections opened after they are ready, and these clients never reconnect.

choices.label: The new pods are failing readiness, so the Service ignores them
choices.feedback: Possible in general, but the connection pattern alone explains it here.

choices.label: The Service needs a restart to notice the new endpoints
choices.feedback: Endpoints update on their own; the existing connections are what does not move.

interactive.reveal: Balance per request in the gRPC client over the endpoint list, or set a maximum connection age so clients reconnect and spread across new pods.

title: Cluster Upgrades: Version Skew, Drains and Disruption Budgets
objectives: Plan a cluster upgrade in the right order, within the supported version skew
Explain how a node drain evicts pods and how disruption budgets slow or block it
Choose between surge upgrades and a new node pool, and estimate how long an upgrade takes

cards.title: Why upgrades never stop
cards.body: Kubernetes ships a minor release roughly three times a year, and each one gets about a year of patch support upstream; managed services publish their own, similar support windows. A cluster left alone falls out of support within about a year and then has to jump several versions under pressure. Teams that upgrade every release, one minor version at a time, keep each step small and practised.

cards.title: Order and skew: control plane first
cards.body: Upgrade the control plane first, then the nodes. The kubelet on a node may be older than the API server, up to three minor versions behind on recent releases, but never newer, so nodes can lag while you roll them. Before starting, check the release notes for APIs removed in the target version: manifests, charts and controllers that still use a removed API version fail to apply after the upgrade, even though the cluster itself looks healthy.

cards.title: Draining one node
cards.body: Every eviction asks the disruption budget first.
steps: Cordon the node so no new pods are scheduled on it
Request an eviction for each pod on the node
The API server checks the pod’s disruption budget
Allowed: the pod gets SIGTERM and its grace period, and its controller recreates it elsewhere
Refused: the drain waits and retries until the budget allows it
When the node is empty, upgrade or replace it

cards.title: Worked example: a 30-node surge upgrade
cards.body: A node pool of 30 nodes is upgraded with a surge of 3: three new nodes are added, three old nodes are drained and removed, and so on. If each batch takes about 10 minutes to boot, drain and delete, the pool needs 30 ÷ 3 = 10 batches, and 10 × 10 = 100 minutes. Raising the surge to 6 roughly halves the time but needs quota for 6 extra nodes and doubles how many pods move at once.

cards.title: Trap: a budget that never lets anything go
cards.body: A service runs 2 replicas with a disruption budget of minAvailable 2, or maxUnavailable 0. Every eviction is refused, so every drain stalls on that node. Managed services wait for a while and then fail the upgrade or force the eviction, depending on the provider. Size budgets so one pod can always go: for example 3 replicas with maxUnavailable 1, spread across zones.

questions.prompt: A cluster runs 1.35 on the control plane and the nodes. You are moving to 1.36. Which order is supported?

choices.label: Upgrade the nodes to 1.36 first, then the control plane
Upgrade the control plane to 1.36, then roll the nodes
Upgrade both at once so that they never differ
Jump the nodes straight to 1.37 while the control plane is upgraded

questions.explanation: Kubelets may lag the API server but must not be newer, so the control plane goes first. Nodes first or nodes at 1.37 would make kubelets newer than the API server, and upgrading everything at once removes the chance to stop if the control plane step goes wrong.

questions.prompt: A drain hangs on one node. The service there has 2 replicas and a disruption budget of minAvailable 2. Why?

choices.label: The node’s kubelet is too old to accept eviction requests
The pods are ignoring SIGTERM, so their grace period never ends
Every eviction would drop below 2 available, so each one is refused
Drains only evict pods that have no disruption budget at all

questions.explanation: With minAvailable equal to the replica count, no voluntary eviction is ever allowed, so the drain retries forever. Kubelet version does not affect evictions, a pod ignoring SIGTERM is killed after its grace period, and drains do evict pods with budgets, as long as the budget allows it.

questions.prompt: The cluster upgrade succeeds, but the next deploy fails with “no matches for kind” on an API version. What happened?

choices.label: The deploy used an API version that the new release removed
The new nodes have not pulled the container images yet
The scheduler is still running the previous minor version
The disruption budget blocked the deploy during the upgrade

questions.explanation: Removed API versions are the classic upgrade break: the cluster is fine but old manifests no longer match any kind. Image pulls fail later and differently, the control plane was upgraded as a whole, and disruption budgets limit evictions, not deploys.

questions.prompt: For a critical cluster you want to be able to undo a node upgrade within minutes. Which approach gives that?

choices.label: An in-place upgrade of each node, one at a time
A surge upgrade with a large surge to finish sooner
Pausing the cluster autoscaler during the surge upgrade
A new node pool on the new version, keeping the old pool for now

questions.explanation: With a new pool beside the old one, undoing means moving pods back to nodes that still exist. In-place and surge upgrades replace the old nodes as they go, so a rollback is another full upgrade, and pausing the autoscaler changes nothing about reversibility.

questions.prompt: A node pool of 30 nodes is upgraded 3 nodes at a time. Each batch takes about 10 minutes to add, drain and remove. How long does the pool take?
assumptions: Batches run one after another
No drain is blocked by a disruption budget
questions.explanation: Sanity check: one batch alone is 10 minutes, and one node at a time would be 300; a blocked drain adds its full wait to whichever batch it hits.

questions.prompt: Order a minor-version cluster upgrade.

items.label: Upgrade the control plane
Roll each node pool, draining nodes within their budgets
Check release notes and fix uses of removed APIs
Verify workloads and remove the old nodes
Upgrade cluster add-ons that must match the version

questions.explanation: Fix removed APIs before anything moves, then control plane, add-ons, nodes, and verification.

flashcards.back: Control plane first, then nodes; kubelets may lag the API server but must not be newer.
Cordons the node, then evicts each pod through the eviction API, which checks disruption budgets.

flashcards.front: A budget that blocks every drain?
flashcards.back: minAvailable equal to replicas, or maxUnavailable 0; leave room for one pod to go.

sources.title: Google Cloud: Node pool upgrade strategies

mechanism.title: How a cluster is upgraded without an outage
steps: Prepare first. Read the release notes for the target minor version, list removed and deprecated APIs, and scan manifests, charts and the live cluster for them. Check that add-ons such as the network plugin, DNS, ingress controller and storage drivers support the new version. Upgrade a staging cluster first and run the same checks there, because removed APIs are the most common cause of a successful upgrade followed by failed deploys.

Upgrade the control plane next. On a managed service this is one operation; the provider replaces the API servers and controllers while the API stays reachable. The version skew policy then lets nodes stay behind: a kubelet may be older than the API server, by up to three minor versions on current releases, but never newer. That gap is what allows nodes to be rolled gradually after the control plane is done.

Each node is replaced by draining it. A drain cordons the node so nothing new lands there, then evicts every pod through the eviction API. Each eviction is checked against the pod’s disruption budget, which states how many replicas must stay available or may be unavailable. Allowed evictions terminate the pod with its normal grace period, and its controller recreates it on another node; refused evictions are retried until enough replicas are ready elsewhere.

Surge upgrades add a few new nodes, drain the same number of old ones, and repeat; maxSurge and maxUnavailable trade speed against extra capacity and disruption. A blue-green node pool creates a full pool on the new version, moves workloads by cordoning and draining the old pool, and keeps the old nodes for a soak period, which makes undoing quick at the cost of running two pools for a while.

Disruption budgets must allow progress. A budget that permits zero disruptions blocks every drain; managed services wait for a provider-specific time, then fail the upgrade or force the eviction. Good budgets leave room for one replica to go, and pair with enough replicas spread across zones and readiness probes that only pass when a pod can really serve. Single-replica workloads cannot be both protected and drained, so they need a maintenance window or a second replica.

useWhen: Every cluster, every minor release: small regular upgrades instead of rare forced jumps.
Production services with disruption budgets that leave room for one replica to move.
avoidWhen: Avoid skipping minor versions on the control plane; upgrade one minor at a time.
Avoid budgets of zero allowed disruptions, and in-place upgrades where a fast undo matters.

rows: Move pods back to the old pool
A whole second pool for a while

numbers.title: How long a node pool upgrade takes
assumptions: 30 nodes, surge of 3
About 10 minutes per batch to boot, drain and delete
One blocked drain waits 60 minutes before the provider forces it, illustrative
steps: Batches: 30 ÷ 3 = 10.
Normal time: 10 × 10 = 100 minutes.
One blocked drain adds its 60-minute wait to one batch: about 160 minutes in total.
numbers.result: Surge size sets the pace, but a single badly sized disruption budget can add more time than the rest of the upgrade combined.

india.title: Upgrade rules in the Kubernetes docs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Kubernetes version skew policy says the kubelet must not be newer than the API server and may be up to three minor versions older, and that the control plane is upgraded before nodes. The safe-drain task describes cordoning and evicting through the eviction API, which respects disruption budgets. Google Cloud documents surge and blue-green node pool upgrade strategies for managed clusters.

pitfalls.trap: “We will upgrade the cluster when we have to.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d upgrade every minor release, one version at a time, so each step is small and practised.”

pitfalls.trap: “Set the budget to zero disruptions so the service is always safe.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d allow one pod to go and run enough replicas; a zero budget blocks every drain.”

takeaways: Upgrade the control plane first; kubelets may lag but never lead.
Find and fix removed APIs before the upgrade, not after.
Drains evict through disruption budgets; size budgets so one pod can always move.
Surge for speed; a new node pool when a fast undo matters.

interactive.title: The upgrade that stopped at node 7
interactive.prompt: A surge upgrade of a 20-node pool has been stuck on node 7 for 40 minutes. Node 7 runs one pod of a cache with 1 replica and a disruption budget of minAvailable 1.

choices.label: The eviction is refused, because removing the only replica would break minAvailable 1
choices.feedback: Right: with one replica and minAvailable 1, no voluntary eviction is ever allowed.

choices.label: Node 7 is broken and cannot be drained until it is rebooted
choices.feedback: The node is fine; the API server is refusing the eviction.

choices.label: The surge quota ran out, so no new node can be added
choices.feedback: The new nodes already exist; the stall is on emptying the old one.

interactive.reveal: Give the cache a second replica in another zone and set maxUnavailable 1, or schedule a window to drain it deliberately; the provider may otherwise force the eviction after its timeout.

title: Stateful Workloads on Kubernetes: Volumes, StatefulSets and Operators
objectives: Explain what a StatefulSet adds: stable names, a volume per pod and ordered rollouts
Predict how zonal block volumes and the volume binding mode constrain where pods run
Decide between running a database with an operator and using a managed database

cards.title: Claims, volumes and classes
cards.body: A pod asks for storage with a persistent volume claim: a size, an access mode and a storage class. The storage class names a provisioner, usually the cloud’s block or file storage driver, which creates a persistent volume and binds it to the claim. The volume outlives the pod, so a restarted or rescheduled pod mounts the same data. The class’s reclaim policy decides whether deleting the claim also deletes the disk (Delete) or keeps it for manual recovery (Retain).

cards.title: What a StatefulSet adds
cards.body: A Deployment’s pods are interchangeable: random names, shared or no storage, replaced in any order. A StatefulSet gives each pod a stable ordinal name such as db-0, db-1 and db-2, a stable DNS name through a headless Service, and its own claim from a volume claim template, so db-1 always comes back with db-1’s disk. Rolling updates replace one pod at a time, from the highest ordinal down, waiting for each to be ready before moving on.

cards.title: Misconception: a StatefulSet makes the database highly available
cards.body: A StatefulSet keeps identity and storage attached to each pod; it knows nothing about replication, leader election, failover or backups. If db-0 is the primary and its node dies, the StatefulSet recreates db-0 and reattaches its disk, which can take minutes, but promoting a replica in the meantime is the database’s job, or an operator’s. Three replicas only help if the database itself replicates between them.

cards.title: Where a zonal volume lets a pod run
cards.body: The disk lives in one zone, so the pod must too.
steps: A pod with a claim is created; with delayed binding, no disk exists yet
The scheduler picks a node, taking the pod’s other constraints into account
The provisioner creates the disk in that node’s zone and binds it
Later the pod is rescheduled: only nodes in the disk’s zone qualify
If that zone has no capacity, the pod stays Pending
Recovery in another zone needs a snapshot restore or database replication

cards.title: Trap: binding the disk before the pod is placed
cards.body: With immediate binding, the disk is created as soon as the claim exists, in whichever zone the provisioner picks. The scheduler must then put the pod in that zone, even if the pod’s spread rules or the free capacity point elsewhere, and pods can stay Pending. Storage classes for zonal disks should use the WaitForFirstConsumer binding mode, so the disk is created in the zone of the node the pod was scheduled to.

cards.title: Operators: running a database as code
cards.body: An operator is a controller plus custom resources that encode how to run one piece of software: create a primary and replicas, fail over, take backups, upgrade versions. You declare a cluster resource, and the operator reconciles towards it, much like a Deployment controller does for pods. A good operator makes self-run databases workable, but your team still owns its upgrades, its bugs and every 3 a.m. failover. A managed database moves that work to the provider.

questions.prompt: Why run a three-node database cluster as a StatefulSet rather than a Deployment?

choices.label: Each pod keeps a stable name and its own volume across restarts
A StatefulSet replicates the data between the three pods
A StatefulSet can only be scheduled on nodes with local disks
It promotes a replica to primary when the leader fails

questions.explanation: Stable identity and one volume per pod are what a StatefulSet provides. Replication and promotion are the database’s or an operator’s job, and StatefulSets work with any storage class, network disks included.

questions.prompt: A database pod’s node fails. The pod is recreated but stays Pending, although other zones have plenty of free nodes. Why?

choices.label: The StatefulSet waits for an operator to approve the new pod
Its zonal disk can only attach to nodes in the original zone
The scheduler never reschedules a pod that owns a volume
The new pod must keep the same IP address as the old one

questions.explanation: A block volume lives in one zone, so the pod can only run there, and that zone has no room. No approval is needed, pods with volumes are rescheduled normally within the volume’s zone, and pod IPs are allowed to change.

questions.prompt: A team deletes the claim for a test database, and the cloud disk disappears with it. Which setting caused that?

choices.label: The claim’s access mode was ReadWriteOnce
The volume binding mode was WaitForFirstConsumer
The storage class reclaim policy was Delete
The StatefulSet was set to roll pods in order

questions.explanation: With reclaim policy Delete, removing the claim deletes the volume and its disk; Retain would have kept it. Access mode controls how many nodes can mount it, binding mode controls when it is created, and pod ordering does not touch volumes.

questions.prompt: A small team with no database specialists needs PostgreSQL for one service. What is usually the better choice?

choices.label: A StatefulSet of three pods with the stock PostgreSQL image
A database operator in the cluster, managed by the team
One pod with a volume, and backups when someone remembers
The cloud provider’s managed PostgreSQL service

questions.explanation: A managed service hands failover, patching and backups to the provider, which matters most for a team without specialists. A bare StatefulSet has no failover, an operator still leaves the team owning upgrades and incidents, and ad hoc backups are how data is lost.

questions.prompt: A StatefulSet of 5 pods is updated one pod at a time. Each pod takes about 3 minutes to stop, start and become ready again. How long does the rollout take?
assumptions: Pods are replaced strictly one after another
No pod fails its readiness check
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a Deployment with a surge could replace several pods at once, but a StatefulSet waits for each ordinal in turn, so slow-starting databases make long rollouts.

questions.prompt: Order what happens when a pod with a WaitForFirstConsumer claim is first created.

items.label: The provisioner creates a disk in that node’s zone
The claim exists but has no volume yet
The kubelet attaches and mounts the disk, and the pod starts
The scheduler places the pod on a node
The volume is bound to the claim

questions.explanation: Delayed binding lets scheduling pick the zone first, so the disk is created where the pod will run.

flashcards.back: Stable ordinal names, stable DNS, one volume per pod, ordered one-at-a-time rollouts.
Creates the disk only after the pod is scheduled, in that node’s zone.
Delete removes the disk with the claim; Retain keeps it for manual recovery.

mechanism.title: How state survives on a platform built for replaceable pods
steps: Storage is requested, not configured on nodes. A persistent volume claim asks for a size and access mode from a storage class; the class’s provisioner creates a volume, usually a cloud block disk, and binds it one to one with the claim. ReadWriteOnce volumes attach to one node at a time, which suits databases; shared file storage offers ReadWriteMany at lower performance. Expansion, snapshots and encryption come from the driver and class settings.

StatefulSets add identity. Pods get ordinal names, a headless Service gives each a DNS name such as db-1.db, and a volume claim template creates one claim per ordinal. When db-1 is rescheduled it gets db-1’s claim back. Pods are created in order and, by default, updated in reverse order, one at a time, each waiting to be ready. By default the claims stay when the StatefulSet is scaled down or deleted, which protects data but leaves disks to clean up.

Block volumes are zonal. A pod using one can only run in the volume’s zone, so a zone outage or a full zone keeps it Pending. WaitForFirstConsumer binding creates the volume after scheduling, which keeps spread and capacity decisions with the scheduler. Surviving a zone loss therefore needs replication at the database level across pods in different zones, or restoring a snapshot into another zone, which costs time and recent writes.

The database still has to be operated: replication, leader election, failover, backups, version and schema upgrades, and connection routing to the current primary. Operators package that knowledge as a controller with custom resources, and the mature ones handle failover and backups well. They also add a component to upgrade and debug, and a failure mode where the operator itself is broken during an incident.

Managed database services take on failover, patching, backups and storage scaling, with documented recovery behaviour, in exchange for less control and a higher unit price. For most teams the sensible default is a managed database, with Kubernetes running the stateless tiers; self-running on Kubernetes makes sense when a team has the skills, needs an engine or version the provider lacks, or must run the same stack everywhere.

useWhen: Stateful software that needs stable identity and its own disk, with a mature operator.
Platforms that must run the same database stack on several clouds or on premises.
avoidWhen: Avoid self-running critical databases without the skills to own failover and upgrades.
Avoid assuming a StatefulSet replicates data or survives a zone loss on its own.

rows: Pods wait for the zone; no failover
Operator promotes a replica in another zone
Provider fails over to a standby

numbers.title: Time to recover a primary in a failed zone
assumptions: Primary in zone A on a zonal disk; replicas in B and C
Zone A is down for 2 hours
Illustrative timings
steps: Without failover: the primary waits for zone A, so writes stop for about 120 minutes.
Operator or managed failover: detect in about 1 minute, promote a replica in about 1 minute, reconnect clients in about 1 minute.
Writes resume after about 3 minutes, losing at most the replication lag if replication was asynchronous.
numbers.result: A StatefulSet alone ties recovery to the zone; replication plus automated failover turns a two-hour outage into minutes.

india.title: Storage and StatefulSets in the docs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The Kubernetes documentation describes StatefulSets as giving pods sticky identities and stable storage, updating them in reverse ordinal order by default, and keeping their claims when pods are deleted or scaled down. The storage class page documents reclaim policies and recommends WaitForFirstConsumer for topology-constrained volumes, so the volume is provisioned according to the pod’s scheduling constraints. The operator pattern page explains operators as controllers with custom resources.

pitfalls.trap: “It runs as a StatefulSet, so the database is highly available.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check what replicates the data and who promotes a replica; the StatefulSet only keeps identity and disks.”

pitfalls.trap: “Our database pod can move to any zone if one fails.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check the disk: a zonal volume pins the pod, so we need replication across zones.”

takeaways: Claims request storage; the class decides the provisioner, binding mode and reclaim policy.
StatefulSets give stable names and one disk per pod, not replication.
Zonal disks pin pods to a zone; use WaitForFirstConsumer and replicate across zones.
Default to a managed database unless you can own an operator and its failovers.

interactive.title: Scaling a StatefulSet down and up
interactive.prompt: A StatefulSet of 4 pods, db-0 to db-3, is scaled down to 2 and, a week later, back up to 4. The claims use the default retention settings.

choices.label: db-2 and db-3 come back with their old disks and last week’s data
choices.feedback: Right: by default the claims stay when you scale down, and the same ordinals reattach them.

choices.label: db-2 and db-3 get new, empty disks, because their claims were deleted
choices.feedback: That needs a retention policy that deletes claims on scale-down, which is not the default.

choices.label: The scale-up fails until the old claims are deleted by hand
choices.feedback: The old claims are reused, not in the way.

interactive.reveal: Stale replicas rejoin with week-old data, so the database must resync them; delete or reset the claims on purpose if you want fresh replicas.
