Scheduling rules that decide which zone a volume ends up in
Backups and restores that still matter when volumes persist

title: Connecting Networks: Peering, Transit Hubs, Private Endpoints and Hybrid Links
objectives: Explain why peering is not transitive and why address ranges must not overlap
Choose between a peering mesh and a transit hub as the number of networks grows
Reach managed services through private endpoints, and pick VPN or a dedicated link to on-premises

cards.title: Peering joins two networks, and only two
cards.body: Peering connects two virtual networks so their private addresses can reach each other over the provider’s backbone, with no gateway in the path. It has two rules that shape every design. Ranges must not overlap, because a route cannot point to the same addresses in two places. And peering is not transitive: if A peers with B and B with C, A still cannot reach C through B. Each pair that must talk needs its own peering.

cards.title: Worked example: ten networks
cards.body: Ten networks that all need to reach each other need a peering for every pair: 10 × 9 = 90 ordered pairs, halved to 45 peerings, each with route table entries on both sides. Add an eleventh network and that is 10 more. A transit hub, a managed router that networks attach to, needs 10 attachments and one place for route tables, inspection and logging, at the cost of an extra hop and a per-gigabyte processing charge.

cards.title: Private access to a managed service
cards.body: The service appears as an address inside your own network.
steps: The provider’s service, or a partner’s, publishes an endpoint service
You create a private endpoint in your subnet; it gets a private IP
Private DNS maps the service hostname to that private IP
Your app calls the usual hostname and the traffic stays on the provider network
No NAT gateway, internet gateway or public IP is involved
Policies on the endpoint can limit which resources it reaches

cards.title: Private endpoints for managed services
cards.body: Managed services such as object storage, queues and databases have public endpoints by default, so private servers reach them through a NAT gateway and pay its processing charge. A private endpoint puts the service on a private IP in your own network, so traffic never touches the internet path and the service can be locked to accept calls only through that endpoint. Names are the usual catch: private DNS must resolve the service hostname to the endpoint, or clients silently keep using the public path.

cards.title: Reaching on-premises: VPN or a dedicated link
cards.body: A site-to-site VPN runs encrypted tunnels over the internet. It is quick to set up and cheap, but throughput per tunnel is limited to a few gigabits per second at most, and latency varies with the internet path. A dedicated interconnect is a private circuit from your data centre or a colocation site into the provider, with steady latency and 10 or 100 gigabit ports, but it takes weeks to order. Many teams run a VPN as the backup path for the dedicated link.

cards.title: Trap: every team picked 10.0.0.0/16
cards.body: Each team created its network with the console’s default range. Two years later they need to connect, and every network overlaps with every other, so peering and routing are impossible without renumbering or address translation. Plan address space centrally from the start: one non-overlapping block per network, room for growth, and on-premises ranges excluded.

questions.prompt: Network A peers with B, and B peers with C. Can a server in A reach a server in C?

choices.label: Yes, traffic is forwarded through B’s routing table
Only if B runs a NAT gateway for the other two networks
Yes, as long as the three address ranges do not overlap
No; A and C need a peering of their own, or a shared hub

questions.explanation: Peering is not transitive, so A to C needs its own peering or a transit hub. B’s routes do not forward peered traffic, a NAT gateway in B does not route peered traffic, and non-overlapping ranges are necessary but not sufficient.

questions.prompt: Two teams’ networks both use 10.0.0.0/16, and now they must connect. What is the core problem?

choices.label: Peering requires both networks to be in the same region
Routes cannot send the same addresses to two places
The networks need the same security group names first
Peering only works between networks in one account

questions.explanation: Overlapping ranges make routing ambiguous, so peering is refused; renumbering or translation is required. Cross-region and cross-account peering are both widely supported, and security group names have nothing to do with routing.

questions.prompt: Private servers upload terabytes to the provider’s object storage through a NAT gateway, and the NAT bill is large. What fixes it?

choices.label: A private endpoint for object storage inside the network
A bigger NAT gateway so the traffic costs less per gigabyte
Public IPs on the servers so they can skip the NAT gateway
A VPN tunnel between the network and the storage service

questions.explanation: A private endpoint keeps the traffic on a private path, so it no longer goes through the NAT gateway. NAT pricing is per gigabyte whatever the size, public IPs expose the servers, and a VPN is for connecting networks, not for reaching a provider service.

questions.prompt: A factory must send a steady 8 Gbps to the cloud with predictable latency, for years. Which link fits?

choices.label: A single site-to-site VPN tunnel over the internet
Peering between the factory network and the cloud network
A dedicated interconnect, with a VPN as the backup path
Public endpoints with TLS from the factory over the internet

questions.explanation: Steady high throughput and predictable latency are what a dedicated circuit offers, and a VPN behind it covers circuit failures. One VPN tunnel tops out at a few gigabits with variable latency, peering connects cloud networks rather than sites, and the public internet gives no latency promise.

questions.prompt: Twelve networks must all reach each other. How many peerings does a full mesh need?
assumptions: Every pair needs exactly one peering
No network is reached through another
questions.explanation: Design implication: a transit hub would need 12 attachments instead of 66 peerings, and each new network adds one attachment rather than 12 more peerings.

questions.prompt: A company runs 15 networks across teams, plus a data-centre link, and adds a few networks each quarter.
constraints: Security wants one place to inspect traffic between networks
Network changes must not need edits in every network
A small extra hop is acceptable

approaches.label: Peer every pair of networks directly
Attach every network and the data-centre link to a transit hub
Merge all teams into one large shared network

rationaleOptions.label: New networks need one attachment, not a peering to each other network
A mesh is cheaper at any size because it has no processing charge
Routing, inspection and the on-premises link sit in one place
One shared network removes the need for any access control

rationaleConflicts.r3: Peering avoids the hub’s charge, but 105 peerings and their routes cost far more in operations, and give no central inspection point.
rationaleConflicts.r4: A single network still needs segmentation, and merges every team’s blast radius into one.

questions.explanation: At this size a hub keeps routing and inspection central and makes each new network one attachment; a full mesh would already need 105 peerings.

flashcards.back: Ranges must not overlap, and peering is not transitive.
n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 peerings; a hub needs n attachments.
Private DNS must resolve the service name to the endpoint, or traffic stays on the public path.

sources.title: AWS: What is a transit gateway?
Microsoft Learn: What is Azure Private Link?

mechanism.title: How cloud networks are joined to each other and to the rest of the world
steps: Start with address planning. Every network that may ever connect to another, including on-premises ranges and partner networks, needs a range that overlaps with none of them. A central plan that hands out blocks per account and region, with room to grow, avoids the most expensive networking mistake, which is discovering overlaps when two networks must finally talk.

Peering links two networks directly over the provider backbone. Traffic stays private, there is no extra hop, and peered traffic is billed at internal transfer rates, often free within one zone. Peering is not transitive, so it suits a few networks or a few specific pairs. Each side still controls access with security rules, and route tables on both sides must point the peer’s range at the peering.

A transit hub, offered by each major provider under its own name, is a managed router: networks, VPNs and dedicated links attach to it, and its route tables decide who can reach whom. It scales linearly with the number of networks, gives one place to put inspection firewalls and flow logs, and can separate environments with different route tables. It adds an extra hop and a per-gigabyte processing charge.

Private endpoints bring a managed or partner service into your network as a private IP. Calls to object storage, queues, secrets or a SaaS vendor stay on the provider network, skip the NAT gateway and its charges, and the service can refuse anything that does not arrive through the endpoint. Private DNS zones make the normal hostname resolve to the endpoint, which is the step most often missed.

Hybrid links connect sites. A site-to-site VPN uses IPsec tunnels over the internet, is ready in minutes and suits modest or backup traffic. A dedicated interconnect is a physical circuit at 10 or 100 gigabits per second with stable latency, ordered through the provider or a partner at a colocation site. Routes are exchanged dynamically with BGP, and production designs use two circuits in different locations, or a circuit plus a VPN, so one failure does not cut the site off.

useWhen: Organisations with several accounts, environments or teams that need controlled private connectivity.
Workloads that move a lot of data to managed services or to on-premises systems.
avoidWhen: Avoid full peering meshes beyond a handful of networks.
Avoid default address ranges for any network that may ever connect to another.

rows: No hop; routes on both sides
VPN: limited; circuit: weeks to order

numbers.title: Mesh vs hub as networks grow
assumptions: 15 networks today, 25 within two years
Every network must reach every other
Counts only; prices vary by provider
steps: Mesh today: 15 × 14 = 210, halved is 105 peerings.
Mesh at 25: 25 × 24 = 600, halved is 300 peerings.
Hub: 15 attachments today and 25 later, one per network.
numbers.result: A mesh grows with the square of the network count while a hub grows linearly, which is why most organisations switch to a hub before about ten networks.

india.title: Peering and private access in provider docs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: AWS documents that VPC peering connections do not support transitive peering and cannot connect networks with overlapping ranges, and describes a transit gateway as a regional hub connecting networks and on-premises links. Google Cloud’s Private Service Connect and Azure Private Link both expose services on private IP addresses inside a consumer network, so traffic does not traverse the public internet.

pitfalls.trap: “B is peered with both, so A can reach C through it.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d add an A–C peering or a hub; peering is not transitive.”

pitfalls.trap: “We’ll pick address ranges when we need to connect.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d plan non-overlapping ranges now; renumbering later is far more expensive.”

takeaways: Peering is not transitive, and ranges must never overlap; plan addresses centrally.
A mesh needs n × (n − 1) ÷ 2 peerings; a hub needs n attachments.
Private endpoints keep service traffic off NAT and the internet; fix private DNS.
VPN for quick or backup links; dedicated interconnect for steady, high throughput.

interactive.title: The private endpoint nobody used
interactive.prompt: A team creates a private endpoint for the storage service, but the NAT gateway bill does not change. The servers still call storage.example-cloud.com.

choices.label: The hostname still resolves to the public address, so traffic still goes through NAT
choices.feedback: Right: without private DNS for the service name, clients never learn the endpoint’s private IP.

choices.label: Private endpoints only take effect after the servers are rebooted
choices.feedback: Nothing on the servers needs a restart; name resolution decides the path.

choices.label: The storage service blocks endpoints until the bucket is made public
choices.feedback: Endpoints are for private access; making the bucket public is the opposite of the goal.

interactive.reveal: Attach a private DNS zone so the service hostname resolves to the endpoint, then confirm with a lookup from a server and watch NAT traffic fall.

seeAlso.why: The single network, subnets and NAT gateway this lesson connects together
CIDR ranges, which must not overlap between networks
Data transfer and NAT charges that private paths reduce

title: Cloud Quotas and Limits: The Capacity You Do Not Own
objectives: Tell adjustable quotas from hard limits, and find the ones a design depends on
Handle API throttling with backoff, jitter and lower concurrency
Plan quota headroom for scaling events, failover regions and IP address space

cards.title: Two kinds of ceiling
cards.body: Every cloud account has ceilings per region: how many vCPUs of each instance family, load balancers, addresses, function concurrency, API calls per second. Most are adjustable quotas, set low by default to protect new accounts and the provider, and raised on request, sometimes within minutes and sometimes after days of review. Some are hard limits fixed by the service’s design, such as a maximum object size or rules per security group, and those must shape the design itself.

cards.title: Throttling is a quota on API calls
cards.body: Control-plane APIs, the ones that create instances, update DNS or read secrets, are rate limited per account, often with a token bucket that allows short bursts. Exceed it and calls fail with a throttling error. A deploy tool firing 300 parallel calls, or every pod reading a secret at start-up, can trip it. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, lower the concurrency, and cache what you read, rather than retrying immediately and making it worse.

cards.title: Finding the limits before an incident does
cards.body: Quota work is part of capacity planning.
steps: List the resources a scale-up or failover would create
Look up the quota for each in every region you might use
Compare the peak or failover need with the quota
Request increases ahead of time, and record them as code where possible
Alert when usage passes about 80% of any quota
Re-check after every architecture change or new region

cards.title: Worked example: pods that eat subnet addresses
cards.body: Some Kubernetes network plugins give every pod an address from the cloud subnet. A /22 subnet holds 1,024 addresses, and the provider reserves a few, here 5, leaving 1,019. If each node uses 1 address for itself and 30 for pods, that is 31 per node, so the subnet fits 1,019 ÷ 31 ≈ 32 nodes. An autoscaler that wants node 33 fails with an address error, even though the vCPU quota has plenty of room.

cards.title: Trap: the failover region with default quotas
cards.body: The disaster recovery plan says to start 200 instances in the second region. That region has never run more than 10, so its quota is still at the default, and the failover stops at the first quota error during the worst hour of the year. Failover regions need the same quotas as production, tested by actually launching at scale in a game day, not by reading the plan.

questions.prompt: Which is usually an adjustable quota rather than a hard limit of the service?

choices.label: The maximum size of one object in object storage
The number of vCPUs an account may run in a region
The maximum length of a function’s single run
The maximum number of rules in one security group

questions.explanation: Regional vCPU quotas exist to protect accounts and the provider, and are raised on request. Object size, maximum run time and rules per group come from how each service is built and are fixed, or adjustable only within narrow bounds.

questions.prompt: A deploy script makes 300 parallel calls to the cloud API and many fail with throttling errors. What is the right fix?

choices.label: Retry each failed call immediately until it succeeds
Run the script from several machines to spread the calls
Back off exponentially with jitter and lower the concurrency
Switch the script to a different region’s API endpoint

questions.explanation: Backoff with jitter spreads retries out, and lower concurrency stays under the rate limit. Immediate retries add load to an exhausted bucket, the limit is per account so more machines do not help, and another region’s endpoint manages different resources.

questions.prompt: During a regional outage, the failover to the second region stops after 10 instances with a quota error. What should have been done?

choices.label: Raise the second region’s quotas to the failover need, and test it
Use larger instances in the failover region to need fewer of them
Keep the failover runbook short so it starts sooner
Request the quota increase as the first step of the failover

questions.explanation: Quotas must already match the failover need, proven by a real test launch. Larger instances still count against the vCPU quota, a shorter runbook does not change the ceiling, and an increase requested mid-outage may take longer than the outage.

questions.prompt: The node autoscaler fails with “insufficient free addresses in subnet” while the vCPU quota is only half used. What is happening?

choices.label: The provider has run out of capacity for that instance type
The cluster has hit its maximum number of nodes
The subnet’s security group rules limit the number of nodes
Pods and nodes have used up the subnet’s address range

questions.explanation: When pods take subnet addresses, the range runs out before compute does. A capacity shortage gives a different error, a node maximum is not about addresses, and security group rules do not consume or limit addresses.

questions.prompt: A /22 subnet has 1,024 addresses, and the provider reserves 5. Each node needs 1 address plus 30 for its pods. How many nodes fit?
assumptions: Every pod gets a subnet address
Nothing else uses the subnet
questions.explanation: Design implication: a /24 would hold only 8 such nodes, so size pod subnets for the largest cluster you expect, or use a plugin mode that gives pods addresses from a separate range.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to make a planned launch-day scale-up safe from quota errors.

items.label: Request increases well before the event
Look up the quota for each in each region
Test by launching at the planned scale
List every resource the scale-up will create
Compare the peak need with each quota

questions.explanation: Inventory, look up, compare, raise early, then prove it with a real launch.

flashcards.back: A quota is a default ceiling you can raise; a hard limit is part of the service design.
Exponential backoff with jitter, lower concurrency, and caching reads.
Raise them to match production ahead of time, and prove it with a launch test.

sources.title: Microsoft Learn: Azure subscription and service limits, quotas and constraints
AWS: IP addressing for your VPCs and subnets

mechanism.title: How quotas shape capacity planning
steps: The cloud looks unlimited, but each account has ceilings per region and per resource. Quotas cover running vCPUs by instance family, GPUs, addresses, load balancers, managed database instances, function concurrency, storage volumes and more. They start at conservative defaults and are raised through a request, which may be approved automatically or sent for review, especially for scarce resources such as GPUs.

Hard limits are different: they come from how a service is built, such as the largest object or message, the longest function run, or the most rules in one security group, and requests do not move them, or only within narrow bounds. A design that needs more than a hard limit must change, for example by splitting objects, chaining functions or using more groups. Read the limits pages for every service a design depends on before building on it.

Control-plane APIs are rate limited too, per account and often per action, using token buckets that refill at a steady rate and allow bursts. Throttling errors appear during deploys, large autoscaling events and start-up storms, when hundreds of instances or pods call the same API at once. Clients should retry with exponential backoff and jitter, cap their own concurrency and cache results; the provider SDKs do some of this by default, and custom tooling must do it too.

Addresses are a quiet quota. Subnets have fixed sizes, providers reserve a few addresses in each, and some network plugins give every pod a subnet address. Load balancers, endpoints and managed services also take addresses in your subnets. Size subnets for peak node and pod counts with growth, keep spare ranges in the plan, and watch free addresses per subnet as a metric like any other capacity.

Treat quotas as part of capacity planning. For each scaling event and failover plan, list the resources it creates, compare with the quotas in every region involved, raise them in advance, and alert at around 80% of each. Some providers let quota requests be managed through infrastructure as code or organisation templates, so new accounts start with the right ceilings. Prove failover quotas with a launch test, because a quota error in the middle of an incident has no quick fix.

useWhen: Before launches, sales events, new regions and any disaster recovery test.
Accounts where autoscaling or failover may create many resources quickly.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating default quotas as capacity; they are a starting point.
Avoid immediate, unbounded retries against throttled control-plane APIs.

rows: Raise ahead of need, alert at 80%
Size subnets for peak, add ranges

numbers.title: Quota needed for a failover
assumptions: Production peak: 120 instances of 8 vCPUs
Failover region default quota: 256 vCPUs
Illustrative sizes
steps: Failover need: 120 × 8 = 960 vCPUs.
Default quota covers 256 ÷ 8 = 32 instances, about a quarter of the need.
Raise the quota to about 1,200 vCPUs, the need plus 25% headroom, before the plan is relied on.
numbers.result: A failover plan without matching quotas tops out at a fraction of the load it is meant to carry.

india.title: Quotas in provider documentation
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: AWS Service Quotas, Google Cloud’s quotas documentation and Azure’s subscription and service limits page all distinguish adjustable quotas from fixed limits and describe how to view usage and request increases per region. AWS documents that five addresses in each subnet are reserved, which is why a /24 offers 251 usable addresses rather than 256, a detail that matters when pods draw from subnet ranges.

pitfalls.trap: “It’s the cloud, we can scale to whatever we need.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check the quotas in every region the plan uses and raise them before the event.”

pitfalls.trap: “The deploy failed with throttling, so I added retries.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d add exponential backoff with jitter and lower the concurrency, or the retries make it worse.”

takeaways: Quotas are adjustable defaults; hard limits must shape the design.
Throttling needs backoff with jitter and lower concurrency, not instant retries.
Failover regions need production-sized quotas, proven by a launch test.
Subnet addresses are a quota too; size them for peak nodes and pods.

interactive.title: The sale that hit a wall at 40
interactive.prompt: For a flash sale you set the autoscaler maximum to 120 instances of 8 vCPUs. The region’s vCPU quota for that family is 320. Traffic arrives.

choices.label: Scaling stops at 40 instances with quota errors, far below the maximum
choices.feedback: Right: 320 ÷ 8 = 40 instances; the autoscaler maximum cannot exceed the account quota.

choices.label: The autoscaler reaches 120 instances because its own maximum wins
choices.feedback: The autoscaler can only request; the provider refuses launches above the quota.

choices.label: The provider raises the quota automatically to match the autoscaler
choices.feedback: Increases go through a quota request, which may need review; the autoscaler does not raise them.

interactive.reveal: Compare the autoscaler maximum with the quota for each region and family, request the increase days ahead, and alert at 80% of the quota.

seeAlso.why: Autoscaling, whose maximum is bounded by quotas
Subnet sizes that decide how many addresses exist
Zone and region capacity plans that quotas must match
